issues.explanation: Contradicted by USDA AMS 2010-2011 pilot, residue testing of retail organic produce: USDA's report says organic standards prohibit most synthetic substances but list synthetic pest-control materials allowed in organic crop production: elemental sulfur, insecticidal soap, horticultural oils and copper hydroxide. Contradicted by eu-2021-1165.txt: Annex I of EU Regulation 2021/1165 authorises plant protection active substances for organic production including paraffin oils, lime sulphur, copper hydroxide, copper oxychloride, Bordeaux mixture and the synthetic pyrethroids deltamethrin and lambda-cyhalothrin (in traps only), so EU organic rules do not ban all synthetic pesticides. Contradicted by USDA organic regulations (7 CFR 205): 7 CFR 205.601 lists synthetic substances allowed in organic crop production, among them insecticides (insecticidal soaps, horticultural oils, lime sulfur), copper fungicides and a rodenticide, usually only after preventive practices fail; so not all synthetic pesticides are banned. Present the disagreement: name the studies on each side instead of stating one side as fact.

resolved.explanation: Hyland 2019 and Fagan 2020 report the same intervention: four racially and geographically diverse US families, n = 16 participants, 158 urine samples. The sentence presents them as two single studies showing the same pattern ('in 16 people from four US families ... and in a study of 16 participants'), so a reader counts a replication that is one cohort analysed for different compounds. The package also limits both: Hyland is abstract only, a small uncontrolled pre-post design; Fagan is small and advocacy-funded. Neither limit is stated.
resolved.suggestion: Say it is one small study without a control group, e.g. 'One small study of 16 people in four US families, with no control group, found urinary levels of 13 pesticide compounds fell significantly after an organic diet began, and mean glyphosate fell 70.93 percent within six days.' t3 already labels its rows as the same families.

resolved.explanation: Table t1, introduced by this sentence as the review's count of 'their hazard classes', keeps the rows where the organic column is 0 and drops the two rows of the review's Table 1 where organic-approved substances appear: acutely toxic, 99 of all approved against 3 organic-approved (pyrethrins, and the trap-only pyrethroids lambda-cyhalothrin and deltamethrin), and two PBT criteria fulfilled, 54 against 1 (copper). Those two rows are the evidence behind the claim's 'partly' verdict, so the table reads as a clean sweep the source does not show.

resolved.explanation: This callout names organic-food/organic-produce-carries-lower-pesticide-residues, a qualified claim (not an unresolved one), but drops the condition its verdict notes state: the Baranski meta-analysis's 46% vs 11% rests on only 11 studies that compared frequency, and none allowed a robust comparison of concentrations. The article shows that figure in t2 and says 'the amounts are lower too' in s26 without that limit anywhere. (The Winter and Katz condition, 23% of organic samples with residues, is carried by s25.) The callout's point about legal limits is sound but is a different limit from the one the package gives.

Keep s27 and s28 after it.
